q1: SELECT A.PROJECT_ID, ROUND(AVG(B.EXPERIENCE_YEARS), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM PROJECT AS A INNER JOIN EMPLOYEE AS B ON A.EMPLOYEE_ID = B.EMPLOYEE_ID GROUP BY A.PROJECT_ID
q2: SELECT A.PID AS PROJECT_ID, ROUND(SUM(A.YEARS) / COUNT(A.PID), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM ( SELECT P.PROJECT_ID AS PID, E.EXPERIENCE_YEARS AS YEARS FROM PROJECT P LEFT JOIN EMPLOYEE E ON P.EMPLOYEE_ID = E.EMPLOYEE_ID ) A GROUP BY 1

q2_prompt_sql: SELECT A.PID AS PROJECT_ID, ROUND(SUM(A.YEARS) / COUNT(A.PID), 2) AS AVERAGE_YEARS FROM ( SELECT P.PROJECT_ID AS PID, E.EXPERIENCE_YEARS AS YEARS FROM PROJECT P LEFT JOIN EMPLOYEE E ON P.EMPLOYEE_ID = E.EMPLOYEE_ID ) A GROUP BY 1
counterexample:
INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE (EMPLOYEE_ID, NAME, EXPERIENCE_YEARS) VALUES (1, 'Alice', 5), (2, 'Bob', 10);
INSERT INTO PROJECT (PROJECT_ID, EMPLOYEE_ID) VALUES (1, 1), (1, 2);
explanation: Q1 performs an INNER JOIN between PROJECT and EMPLOYEE, grouping by PROJECT_ID and computing the average of EXPERIENCE_YEARS. Q2 performs a LEFT JOIN and computes the average using SUM(YEARS) / COUNT(PID). The difference arises when there are multiple employees per project in Q2 (LEFT JOIN may return more rows per project than INNER JOIN).
counterexample_dsp: A PROJECT with two employees where one employee has no matching record in EMPLOYEE (but the schema ensures EMPLOYEE_ID references EMPLOYEE, so this won't happen). Alternatively, a scenario where a project has multiple employees but one has NULL in EXPERIENCE_YEARS due to a LEFT JOIN.
